evals.prompt: List the 8 layers of the AWS IAM Policy Evaluation Hierarchy in exact evaluation order, and explain this counter-intuitive production behavior: IAM User `arn:aws:iam::187382368021:user/contractor` has an Identity Policy allowing ONLY `s3:ListBucket` and a Permissions Boundary allowing ONLY `s3:ListBucket`. Yet when a teammate added `"Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::187382368021:user/contractor"}` with `"Action": "s3:GetObject"` to a same-account S3 Bucket Policy, `contractor` was able to download objects (`s3:GetObject`)! Why did the S3 Bucket Policy bypass the IAM User's Permissions Boundary, and how does this differ if the Bucket Policy delegates to `arn:aws:iam::187382368021:root` or a cross-account principal?
evals.expected_output: Lists all 8 layers of the IAM Policy Evaluation Hierarchy in order and explains the Same-Account Resource Policy Asymmetry where a same-account resource policy explicitly naming an IAM User ARN grants access directly without requiring an Identity Policy or Permissions Boundary `Allow` (unless an explicit `Deny` exists).
expectations: Lists the 8 IAM Policy Evaluation layers in order: (1) Explicit Deny in any policy, (2) AWS Organizations SCPs, (3) AWS Organizations RCPs, (4) Resource-Based Policies, (5) IAM Permissions Boundaries, (6) AWS STS Session Policies, (7) Identity-Based Policies, and (8) Implicit Deny

Explains the Same-Account Resource Policy Asymmetry: when a same-account resource policy (S3 Bucket Policy, KMS Key Policy, etc.) explicitly specifies the full IAM User ARN (`arn:aws:iam::187382368021:user/contractor`) in `Principal` rather than the account root (`arn:aws:iam::187382368021:root`), AWS evaluates the resource policy grant directly and can bypass the absence of an `Allow` in the user's Identity Policy and Permissions Boundary unless there is an explicit `Deny`

Contrasts this with cross-account requests or same-account resource policies that name `arn:aws:iam::187382368021:root`, where the intersection of the Identity Policy AND the Permissions Boundary is strictly required
Recommends placing an explicit `Deny` (or moving to IAM Roles + SCPs/RCPs) when enforcing hard guardrails against same-account resource policy grants

evals.prompt: Audit a delegated `PlatformBuilderRole` that has a Permissions Boundary `arn:aws:iam::187382368021:policy/DeveloperBoundary` attached to it and an identity policy allowing: `iam:CreateRole`, `iam:PutRolePolicy`, `iam:CreatePolicyVersion`, `iam:PassRole`, `lambda:CreateFunction`, `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode`, and `ec2:ModifyInstanceAttribute` on `*` with no `Condition` blocks. Classify every privilege escalation path across Classes A, B, C, and D, and provide the exact IAM policy conditions and explicit `Deny` statements required to enforce `DeveloperBoundary` and prevent escalation.
evals.expected_output: Classifies the escalation primitives across Class A (Direct IAM Policy/Credential Manipulation), Class B (`iam:PassRole` + Compute Execution), Class C (Code/Config Modification of Existing Privileged Compute), and Class D (Permission Boundary Bypass via unconditioned `iam:CreateRole`), and provides the exact `iam:PermissionsBoundary` condition and explicit `Deny` statements.
expectations: Classifies Class A (Direct IAM Manipulation: `iam:PutRolePolicy`, `iam:CreatePolicyVersion`), Class B (`iam:PassRole` + `lambda:CreateFunction`), Class C (`lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` on existing privileged functions and `ec2:ModifyInstanceAttribute` injecting `userData` on stopped instances with privileged profiles), and Class D (Permission Boundary Bypass via `iam:CreateRole` without requiring `iam:PermissionsBoundary`)
Shows the mandatory Condition on `iam:CreateRole` (and `iam:CreateUser`): `"StringEquals": {"iam:PermissionsBoundary": "arn:aws:iam::187382368021:policy/DeveloperBoundary"}`

Includes an explicit `Deny` on `iam:DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary`, `iam:DeleteUserPermissionsBoundary`, and `iam:CreatePolicyVersion`/`iam:DeletePolicy` on `arn:aws:iam::187382368021:policy/DeveloperBoundary` itself so the delegated role cannot strip or weaken the boundary
Scopes `iam:PassRole` to specific approved workload role ARNs and `iam:PassedToService`

evals.prompt: We are rolling out an AWS Organizations Data Perimeter across Organization `o-prodorg123`. Explain: (1) the three perimeters of the Data Perimeter Triangle and their exact IAM condition keys, (2) the critical syntax constraints of Resource Control Policies (RCPs) including why detaching `RCPFullAWSAccess` breaks all resource access, and (3) why our Region-Restriction SCP (`aws:RequestedRegion`) broke IAM role creation and CloudFront deployments when we applied it without `NotAction` exemptions.
evals.expected_output: Explains the Data Perimeter Triangle (`aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:ResourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceVpc`/`aws:VpceOrgID`), RCP rules (`RCPFullAWSAccess` base policy + custom RCPs restricted to `Effect: Deny` and `Principal: *` on 5 supported services), and global service `NotAction` exemptions for Region-Restriction SCPs.
expectations: Defines the 3 Data Perimeter invariants: Identity Perimeter (`aws:PrincipalOrgID`), Resource Perimeter (`aws:ResourceOrgID` with `"BoolIfExists": {"aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false"}` exemption), and Network Perimeter (`aws:SourceVpc`, `aws:SourceVpce`, `aws:VpceOrgID`, with `aws:ViaAWSService` exemption)

Explains that AWS Organizations requires the AWS-managed `RCPFullAWSAccess` policy to remain attached to every Root, OU, and Account, and that customer-managed RCPs MUST only contain `"Effect": "Deny"` and `"Principal": "*"` across supported services (`s3`, `sts`, `kms`, `sqs`, `secretsmanager`)

Explains that global AWS services (`iam:*`, `sts:*`, `organizations:*`, `cloudfront:*`, `route53:*`, `waf:*`, `support:*`, `budgets:*`) execute their control plane in `us-east-1`, so a Region-Restriction SCP denying `aws:RequestedRegion != ap-south-1` MUST exempt them in `NotAction` (conditioned on `"BoolIfExists": {"aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false"}`)

evals.prompt:
Audit these two federated identity configurations for privilege escalation:
1. A GitHub Actions IAM OIDC role whose trust policy only has `"StringLike": {"token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:acme-inc/*"}`.
2. An Amazon Cognito Identity Pool role where the IAM trust policy only checks `"StringEquals": {"cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:aud": "ap-south-1:11112222-3333-4444-5555-666677778888"}`, AND the Cognito User Pool App Client allows user self-service updates to `custom:tier` while Identity Pool `RoleMappings` maps `custom:tier == "enterprise-admin"` to an administrative IAM Role.
Explain both escalation attacks and provide the hardened JSON configurations.
evals.expected_output: Explains the GitHub OIDC wildcard `sub` + missing `aud` spoofing vulnerability and the dual Cognito Identity Pool escalation vulnerabilities (missing `:amr == authenticated` unauthenticated bypass + writable `custom:tier` attribute role-mapping escalation), providing the remediated configurations.
expectations: Explains that `"repo:acme-inc/*"` without `:aud` allows any repository, PR, or branch in `acme-inc` to assume the role, and provides the hardened trust policy with `"StringEquals": {"token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com", "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:acme-inc/prod-repo:ref:refs/heads/main"}`

Identifies the first Cognito flaw: omitting `"ForAnyValue:StringLike": {"cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:amr": "authenticated"}` allows unauthenticated (`guest`) identities from the same Identity Pool (`:aud`) to assume the authenticated IAM role

Identifies the second Cognito flaw: when `custom:tier` is in the App Client's `WriteAttributes`, any user can call `UpdateUserAttributes` with their own Access Token to set `custom:tier = "enterprise-admin"` and escalate into the Admin IAM Role via `RoleMappings`
Remediates the Cognito flaw by removing `custom:tier` from `WriteAttributes` on the App Client (or using Cognito User Pool Groups managed only via `AdminAddUserToGroup` for `RoleMappings`)

evals.prompt: We use Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) where developers can read Secrets Manager secrets and stop/start EC2 instances when `"StringEquals": {"aws:ResourceTag/CostCenter": "${aws:PrincipalTag/CostCenter}"}`. How could a developer with `CostCenter=Eng` escalate access to `CostCenter=ExecFinance` resources if tag-governance `Deny` statements are missing, and what exact IAM policy statements prevent tag tampering across resources, principals, and STS sessions?
evals.expected_output: Explains how an attacker modifies `aws:ResourceTag/CostCenter`, `aws:PrincipalTag/CostCenter`, or passes `sts:TagSession` to hijack ABAC matching, and provides the tag-governance `Deny` policy using `aws:RequestTag/CostCenter`, `aws:TagKeys`, and `sts:TagSession`.
expectations: Explains the three ABAC escalation paths: (1) re-tagging a target resource (`ec2:CreateTags` / `secretsmanager:TagResource`) to match the attacker's `CostCenter`, (2) modifying the attacker's own principal tag (`iam:TagRole` / `iam:TagUser`) to `ExecFinance`, or (3) passing session tags (`sts:TagSession`) during `AssumeRole`
Provides an explicit `Deny` statement blocking `iam:TagRole`, `iam:UntagRole`, `iam:TagUser`, `iam:UntagUser`, and `sts:TagSession` for the `CostCenter` key unless authorized

Provides a tag-on-create / tag-modification `Deny` guardrail requiring `"StringNotEquals": {"aws:RequestTag/CostCenter": "${aws:PrincipalTag/CostCenter}"}` and blocking `DeleteTags`/`UntagResource` when `"ForAnyValue:StringEquals": {"aws:TagKeys": ["CostCenter"]}`

evals.prompt: Search AWS documentation to explain AWS IAM Access Analyzer's two analyzer types (`ACCOUNT`/`ORGANIZATION` external access vs `ACCOUNT_UNUSED_ACCESS`/`ORGANIZATION_UNUSED_ACCESS`) and its custom policy check APIs (`CheckNoNewAccess`, `CheckAccessNotGranted`, and `CheckNoPublicAccess`). How do `CheckNoNewAccess` and `CheckAccessNotGranted` differ when validating IAM policies in a CI/CD pipeline?
evals.expected_output: Uses `awsknowledge` to retrieve IAM Access Analyzer documentation, comparing External Access vs Unused Access analyzers and explaining `CheckNoNewAccess`, `CheckAccessNotGranted`, and `CheckNoPublicAccess`.
expectations: Invokes `awsknowledge` (`aws___search_documentation` or `aws___read_documentation`) to look up IAM Access Analyzer analyzer types and custom policy checks

Contrasts External Access analyzers (`ACCOUNT` / `ORGANIZATION`, free, uses automated reasoning to identify resources shared with external principals) with Unused Access analyzers (`ACCOUNT_UNUSED_ACCESS` / `ORGANIZATION_UNUSED_ACCESS`, paid per- principal/finding feature that identifies unused roles, unused access keys, and unused service/action permissions for right-sizing)

Distinguishes the three custom policy check APIs (`access-analyzer` CLI): `CheckNoNewAccess` (compares an updated policy against a reference/baseline policy to verify no new permissions were added), `CheckAccessNotGranted` (verifies a policy does not grant any of a specified list of critical actions/resources), and `CheckNoPublicAccess` (verifies a resource policy does not grant public access)
